children: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation isn't required to return $1.71 billion to creditors of the bankrupt parent company of Silicon Valley Bank, a judge said, dealing a blow to Wall Street investors who bet on winning those funds back.

Judge Beth Labson Freeman of the U.S. District Court in San Jose, Calif., ruled Friday that a liquidation trust for parent company SVB Financial Group can't recover the cash because its officers' "imprudent actions" caused Silicon Valley Bank to suffer at least $5.4 billion in financial damages, offsetting any liability by the FDIC.
The $1.71 billion was cash the parent company had deposited in the subsidiary bank.

Following a $42 billion bank run that prompted regulators to seize Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023, hedge funds and distressed-debt investors acquired SVB Financial's discounted debt ahead of its bankruptcy filing, The Wall Street Journal reported. When the FDIC took over Silicon Valley Bank, the regulator said that depositors would be able to access all of their funds-rather than the standard $250,000 deposit guarantee-but later seized SVB Financial's $1.71 billion deposit.

The liquidation trust later argued in court filings that its creditors relied on the emergency pledge to guarantee all Silicon Valley Bank deposits. The FDIC argued that it was entitled to keep the deposit to cover the costs of the bank failure.

Following a 12-day trial, Judge Freeman found that SVB Financial exercised complete control over the bank's strategy and negligently caused billions of dollars in losses, eliminating the FDIC's obligation to return the deposit. Corporate officers had concentrated more than $100 billion of uninsured deposits into risky fixed-rate securities, stripping $294 million from the bank for stock buybacks despite knowing it was in distress, and terminating interest-rate hedges to boost short-term earnings, according to the decision.

The judge said that negligent risk-taking caused at least $5.4 billion in damages, far exceeding the parent company's $1.71 billion deposit claim. Representatives for the liquidation trust didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

SVB Financial's chapter 11 filing marked the largest U.S. bankruptcy stemming from a bank failure since Washington Mutual in 2008. The collapse of Silicon Valley Bank cost the FDIC's bank-funded Deposit Insurance Fund an estimated $16 billion to $20 billion, according to agency estimates and congressional testimony.
